ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was obtained from Metro South HREC (HREC/2024/QMS/105218).
Methods: We recruited six individuals with TRS who had previously received clozapine: three who ceased clozapine following CIN and three who stopped for reasons unrelated to CIN.
Participants were recruited from Metro South Addiction and Mental Health Services (MSAMHS), a public mental health service in Queensland, Australia.
Eligible participants were recruited if they had a diagnosis of schizophrenia and had a history of previous clozapine treatment.

All participants provided written informed consent, and study procedures were conducted in accordance with the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research (2007).
Participants were classified into two groups according to their history of clozapine treatment.

PBMCs from each participant were seeded at 1.25×10 6 cells/mL in 2 mL of culture medium and incubated under one of three conditions: vehicle control (0.003% DMSO), clozapine (1 µM), or clozapine (1 µM) with N-desmethylclozapine (0.5 µM) and clozapine N-oxide (0.2 µM).

Six participants (aged 22-60 years) with a diagnosis of schizophrenia and a history of previous clozapine treatment were recruited: three were classified into the CIN group (TRS with CIN: 1 female, 2 males), and three into the clozapine-exposed control group (TRS without CIN: 3 males).
Smoking status were also recorded: three participants were smokers (2 TRS with CIN, 1 TRS without CIN) and three were non-smokers (1 TRS with CIN, 2 TRS without CIN).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

)), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p-value = 0.78", "p-value = 0.80"), Sentence = c("Furthermore, cross-group concordance was weak and non significant ( = 0.04, p-value = 0.78) when comparing effect size estimates (log 2 FC) of these significant DE genes between TRS with and without CIN.", "There was no correlation between the log 2 FC of these genes in TRS with CIN and the corresponding estimates in TRS without CIN ( = -0.05, p-value = 0.80)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Background: About one-third of individuals with schizophrenia do not respond to first-line antipsychotics.
Clozapine has superior efficacy for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS), yet remains underutilised partly due to a 1% risk of potentially fatal clozapine-induced neutropenia (CIN).
However, the biological mechanisms underlying CIN remain poorly understood.
Methods: We recruited six individuals with TRS who had previously received clozapine: three who ceased clozapine following CIN and three who stopped for reasons unrelated to CIN.
Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were collected and cultured in vitro under three conditions: untreated, clozapine alone, or clozapine with its two major metabolites.
Single nucleus RNA sequencing was performed to profile the cellular transcriptomic landscape following exposure to clozapine and its metabolites.
Results: After quality control, 59,313 cells spanning 26 distinct clusters were retained.

Multiple cell type-specific genes were differentially expressed in TRS with CIN, or in response to clozapine exposure in TRS donors with CIN (but not in those without CIN), after adjusting for age, sex and smoking status.

We also identified a CIN-associated co-expression module in naïve CD4 T cells that was driven by the transcription factor SREBF1, and robust evidence for differential cell-cell communication involving seven intercellular ligandreceptor pairs.
There was limited evidence that clozapine-related metabolites contributed to these transcriptional changes.
Conclusions: Our findings provide novel insights into cell type-specific transcriptional changes associated with CIN status and/or clozapine exposure in TRS with CIN.
With replication in larger, independent cohorts, this work may contribute to the future development of predictive biomarkers for CIN and safer therapeutic strategies for TRS.
Schizophrenia is a chronic and severe mental illness causing persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, amotivation and cognitive impairments (1).
text.formatted: Schizophrenia is a chronic and severe mental illness causing persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, amotivation and cognitive impairments <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: Symptom onset commonly occurs in early adult life and requires lifelong treatment with antipsychotic medication.
Up to onethird of individuals with schizophrenia will develop treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) that is unresponsive to at least two adequate trials of antipsychotic medications (2, 3).
text.formatted: Up to onethird of individuals with schizophrenia will develop treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) that is unresponsive to at least two adequate trials of antipsychotic medications <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3)</ref>.

text.text: Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with established efficacy in TRS, conferring clinically meaningful benefits in approximately 40% of refractory cases (4).
text.formatted: Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with established efficacy in TRS, conferring clinically meaningful benefits in approximately 40% of refractory cases <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref>.

text.text: Its use is associated with significant improvements in quality of life and reductions in symptom severity, all-cause mortality, suicide risk, and hospitalisation rates (5) (6) (7) (8) (9).
text.formatted: Its use is associated with significant improvements in quality of life and reductions in symptom severity, all-cause mortality, suicide risk, and hospitalisation rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(9)</ref>.

text.text: Despite its established efficacy, fewer than one in four eligible individuals with TRS are ever prescribed clozapine (10).
text.formatted: Despite its established efficacy, fewer than one in four eligible individuals with TRS are ever prescribed clozapine <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10)</ref>.

text.text: A major barrier to clozapine initiation is concern regarding its association with serious adverse drug reactions, particularly a rare, unpredictable, and precipitous decline in neutrophil count, leading to severe neutropenia.

This haematological adverse effect, termed clozapine-induced neutropenia (CIN), occurs in ~1% of individuals given clozapine and most cases manifest within 18 weeks of treatment commencement (11, 12).
text.formatted: This haematological adverse effect, termed clozapine-induced neutropenia (CIN), occurs in ~1% of individuals given clozapine and most cases manifest within 18 weeks of treatment commencement <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">12)</ref>.

text.text: The resultant severe neutropenia confers an increased risk of life-threatening infection, necessitating immediate and often permanent clozapine discontinuation (13).
text.formatted: The resultant severe neutropenia confers an increased risk of life-threatening infection, necessitating immediate and often permanent clozapine discontinuation <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(13)</ref>.

text.text: Currently, clozapine is reserved for TRS and requires strict blood monitoring to detect CIN in the first 18 weeks (e.g., weekly) to two years (e.g., 4-weekly) after clozapine initiation (14).
text.formatted: Currently, clozapine is reserved for TRS and requires strict blood monitoring to detect CIN in the first 18 weeks (e.g., weekly) to two years (e.g., 4-weekly) after clozapine initiation <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(14)</ref>.

text.text: Several jurisdictions including New Zealand and those nations covered by the European Medicines Agency have removed mandates for 4-weekly monitoring after the first two years.

The United States has historically followed a different monitoring schedule, involving weekly monitoring for the first 6 months, fortnightly monitoring from 6 to 12 months, and monthly monitoring thereafter.

Although the FDA formally removed the mandatory clozapine risk evaluation and mitigation strategy in 2025, it continues to recommend absolute neutrophil count monitoring according to the prescribing information (15).
text.formatted: Although the FDA formally removed the mandatory clozapine risk evaluation and mitigation strategy in 2025, it continues to recommend absolute neutrophil count monitoring according to the prescribing information <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(15)</ref>.

text.text: Unfortunately, despite intensive surveillance, the rapid onset of CIN after clozapine commencement in some cases may preclude timely detection, highlighting limitations of current monitoring strategies in fully mitigating this haematological risk (16).
text.formatted: Unfortunately, despite intensive surveillance, the rapid onset of CIN after clozapine commencement in some cases may preclude timely detection, highlighting limitations of current monitoring strategies in fully mitigating this haematological risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(16)</ref>.

text.text: Prior genetic studies support a polygenic architecture for CIN, with association signals implicating loci within the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) region and several T cell-related loci (17) (18) (19) (20).
text.formatted: Prior genetic studies support a polygenic architecture for CIN, with association signals implicating loci within the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) region and several T cell-related loci <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(17)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(18)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(19)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(20)</ref>.

text.text: These findings are consistent with an immune-mediated genetic contribution to CIN susceptibility (21).
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with an immune-mediated genetic contribution to CIN susceptibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(21)</ref>.

text.text: Pharmacological studies suggest that metabolic bioactivation of clozapine yields reactive intermediates capable of directly injuring neutrophils (22) (23) (24).
text.formatted: Pharmacological studies suggest that metabolic bioactivation of clozapine yields reactive intermediates capable of directly injuring neutrophils <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(23)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(24)</ref>.

text.text: Despite these advances, the biological mechanisms driving CIN remain incompletely defined.

A major limitation is that most genomic and mechanistic investigations have relied on bulk level samples, in which modest cell type-specific genetic or transcriptional signals may be diluted or missed when heterogeneous populations from different hematopoietic hierarchy and immune compartments are analysed in aggregate.
To our knowledge, no studies have systematically interrogated the cellular mechanisms underlying CIN and the role of clozapine-related metabolites at single cell resolution.

Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) provide an accessible surrogate for investigating clozapine-associated immune reactivity and have been used in pharmacogenomic and immunological studies of drug response (25).
text.formatted: Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) provide an accessible surrogate for investigating clozapine-associated immune reactivity and have been used in pharmacogenomic and immunological studies of drug response <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(25)</ref>.

text.text: In this study, we therefore used single nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) to profile gene expression in ~60K high-quality cultured PBMCs obtained from six individuals with TRS (three with CIN and three without), exposed in vitro for up to three days to one of three treatments: clozapine alone, clozapine plus its two major metabolites (i.e., N-desmethylclozapine [norclozapine], and clozapine-N-oxide) or untreated.

Our goal was to characterise cell type-specific transcriptional signatures associated with CIN status and with response to both clozapine and the combination of clozapine and its metabolites in TRS donors with and without CIN.

We identified cell type-specific differentially expressed genes, predominantly in naïve CD4 and CD8 T cells, associated with CIN status and/or exposure to clozapine (and its metabolites) in TRS with CIN, but not TRS without CIN.
This specificity extended to broader transcriptional programs, including gene co-expression modules and intercellular communication networks.
Participants were recruited from Metro South Addiction and Mental Health Services (MSAMHS), a public mental health service in Queensland, Australia.
Eligible participants were recruited if they had a diagnosis of schizophrenia and had a history of previous clozapine treatment.

All participants provided written informed consent, and study procedures were conducted in accordance with the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research (2007).
Ethical approval was obtained from Metro South HREC (HREC/2024/QMS/105218).
Participants were classified into two groups according to their history of clozapine treatment.

The CIN group comprised participants who had experienced an absolute neutrophil count <1,500 cells/µL (<1.50×10 9 /L) at any time during clozapine treatment, with no alternative cause for neutropenia identified.
text.formatted: The CIN group comprised participants who had experienced an absolute neutrophil count <1,500 cells/µL (<1.50×10 9 /L) at any time during clozapine treatment, with no alternative cause for neutropenia identified.

text.text: The clozapine-exposed control group comprised participants who had previously received clozapine but had discontinued treatment for reasons other than neutropenia.

Individuals were excluded if they were receiving clozapine at the time of recruitment, had a known active haematological malignancy, or had received cytotoxic or myelosuppressive therapy or other significant cytotoxic exposure within the 12 months preceding study screening.
For each participant, 20 mL of peripheral venous blood was collected into Acid Citrate Dextrose Solution A (ACD-A)-containing blood collection tubes for subsequent isolation of PBMCs.
PBMCs were isolated by Ficoll density-gradient centrifugation using Ficoll-Paque PLUS (Cytiva; cat. no.
Whole blood was diluted 1:1 (v/v) with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), layered over 15 mL Ficoll-Paque PLUS, and centrifuged at 400 × g for 40 min at room temperature.

Collected PBMCs were resuspended in 50 mL PBS and centrifuged at 400 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. Cells were washed in RPMI 1640 (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific; cat. no. 11875-093), centrifuged again under the same conditions, and resuspended in RPMI 1640.
PBMCs were cryopreserved in 50% RPMI 1640, 40% fetal bovine serum (FBS), and 10% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) using a Mr.

Frosty controlled-rate freezing container (Thermo Scientific Nalgene) at -80 °C. Prior to culture, cells were thawed for 1-2 min in a 37 °C water bath, resuspended in RPMI 1640, centrifuged at 400 × g for 10 min at room temperature, and resuspended in complete culture medium consisting of RPMI 1640 supplemented with 10% FBS, 100 U/ml penicillin and 100 μg/ml streptomycin.

PBMCs from each participant were seeded at 1.25×10 6 cells/mL in 2 mL of culture medium and incubated under one of three conditions: vehicle control (0.003% DMSO), clozapine (1 µM), or clozapine (1 µM) with N-desmethylclozapine (0.5 µM) and clozapine N-oxide (0.2 µM).
Clozapine (C6305), N-desmethylclozapine (D5676), and clozapine N-oxide (C0832) were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich.
Concentrations were selected based on preliminary cellviability assays and clinically relevant concentrations of clozapine and its major metabolites (26, 27).
text.formatted: Concentrations were selected based on preliminary cellviability assays and clinically relevant concentrations of clozapine and its major metabolites <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">27)</ref>.

text.text: Cells were incubated for 68h at 37 °C and 5% CO , then harvested and washed in culture medium before resuspension for subsequent processing and single nucleus RNA sequencing.

Cultured PBMC samples were centrifuged at 350 × g for 5 minutes at room temperature, after which the supernatant was removed, and the pellets were resuspended in 1 mL PBS containing 0.04% BSA (A1595, Millipore Sigma).

Cell concentration and viability were assessed using an 8 channel counting slide (ATA Scientific, L72001) and AO/PI reagents (ATA Scientific, F23011) on a Luna FX7 automated cell counter (Logos Biosystems, L70001).
Cells were fixed for 19 hours at 4 °C following the Fixation of Cells & Nuclei for Chromium Fixed RNA Profiling protocol (10X Genomics, CG000478, Rev C), followed by quenching.
text.formatted: Cells were fixed for 19 hours at 4 °C following the Fixation of Cells & Nuclei for Chromium Fixed RNA Profiling protocol (10X Genomics, CG000478, Rev C), followed by quenching.

text.text: Of 18 samples in the study (6 donors × 3 treatment groups), 16 samples were randomly selected for probe hybridization, as the Chromium Fixed RNA Profiling Reagent Kits supports a maximum of 16-plex reactions (10X Genomics, CG000527, Rev F).
Hybridization was carried out for 20 hours at room temperature.
Post hybridization nuclei concentrations were assessed using the same AO/PI based Luna FX7 workflow.
A single pool of post-hybridisation nuclei was generated by determining the sample with the lowest cell count and combining an equal number of cells from all other samples into a single 15 mL tube.
Washing and filtration steps were performed according to the 10X Genomics Protocol CG000527 (Rev F).
We then adjusted the final concentration of the library with post-hybridization resuspension buffer to 6,440 nuclei/µL.

The final suspension was subsequently loaded onto the 10X Genomics Chromium instrument targeting 128,000 nuclei across the pool of 16 samples, and cell capture and library preparation were performed following the Chromium Fixed RNA Profiling Reagent Kits User Guide.
Sequencing was performed at the Australian Genome Research Facility (AGRF) on an Illumina NovaSeq instrument across four S4 flowcell lanes, aiming for a total of 4B reads and >30K reads per nucleus.
text.formatted: Sequencing was performed at the Australian Genome Research Facility (AGRF) on an Illumina NovaSeq instrument across four S4 flowcell lanes, aiming for a total of 4B reads and >30K reads per nucleus.

text.text: The raw FASTQ sequencing data were initially processed using the Cell Ranger (v9.0.0) "multi" algorithm (28).
text.formatted: The raw FASTQ sequencing data were initially processed using the Cell Ranger (v9.0.0) "multi" algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(28)</ref>.

text.text: This pipeline was utilised to demultiplex the sequencing reads per sample, align each sample to the human transcriptome reference, and generate the unique molecular identifier (UMI) count matrix per gene per cell for downstream analyses.
We applied a rigorous data quality control (QC) procedure to each of the 16 individual samples.
Initially, cells expressing fewer than 400 genes and genes that were detectable in fewer than 100 cells were excluded.
Following this, total cell counts were assessed, and cells were removed if they fell outside the range defined by their median cell count ± 3 times the median absolute deviation (MAD).
This criterion was similarly applied to genes, leading to the exclusion of genes with expression levels outside the median ± 3 times the MAD.
To eliminate damaged or apoptotic cells, those with a mitochondrial gene percentage (MT%) greater than 5% cells were excluded.
The Scrublet (v0.2.3) (29) software was employed to estimate the probability that each cell represented a doublet.
We defined the prior probability of the proportion of doublets per sample as 0.8% per sample, following the 10X Genomics protocol guidelines for 16-plex runs.
We then visually inspected the bimodal distribution of doublet scores per sample and manually adjusted the doublet threshold as needed to differentiate single cells from suspected doublets.

After the implementation of stringent multi-QC steps, the raw UMI count matrices were normalised using the SCTransform (v0.4.1) method (30) for each individual dataset, adjusting for MT% and cell cycle scores as covariates.
The normalised data matrices were then integrated utilising the Seurat (v5.2.0) integration workflow (31).
text.formatted: The normalised data matrices were then integrated utilising the Seurat (v5.2.0) integration workflow <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(31)</ref>.

text.text: Next, unsupervised cell type clustering analysis were performed using the standard Seurat pipeline.
Cell types were annotated with the SingleR (v2.2.0) (32) software using recently published scRNA-seq data on 53,981 cultured PBMCs from seven healthy adults as the reference (33).
text.formatted: Cell types were annotated with the SingleR (v2.2.0) (32) software using recently published scRNA-seq data on 53,981 cultured PBMCs from seven healthy adults as the reference <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(33)</ref>.

text.text: Marker genes were selected based on significant differential expression within the target cluster and were subsequently refined by manual cross reference to the CellMarker (v2.0) database (34).
text.formatted: Marker genes were selected based on significant differential expression within the target cluster and were subsequently refined by manual cross reference to the CellMarker (v2.0) database <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(34)</ref>.

text.text: Differential gene expression (DE) analysis was conducted (1) between CIN status groups (i.e., "TRS with CIN vs.

TRS without CIN"), and (2) within each of the CIN groups across three treatment comparisons: "untreated vs. clozapine", "untreated vs. clozapine + metabolites", and "clozapine vs. clozapine + metabolites".
Together, this yielded in a total of seven comparisons (one between group and three within each CIN status group).
For each comparison, DE analyses were performed at the individual cluster level.
Clusters with fewer than 1% of the total cell number were excluded to maintain sufficient statistical power.
The primary DE analysis utilised negative binomial regression, adjusting for covariates including age, sex, smoking status, MT%, and the number of UMIs per cell.
For the comparison between CIN status groups, the model also included treatment group and its interaction with CIN status.

Significant cluster-specific genes were identified based on the criteria that they were expressed in at least 1% of either group of cells, had an absolute log 2 fold change (log 2 FC) greater than 0.25, and possessed a Bonferroni-corrected p-value <0.05.
text.formatted: Significant cluster-specific genes were identified based on the criteria that they were expressed in at least 1% of either group of cells, had an absolute log 2 fold change (log 2 FC) greater than 0.25, and possessed a Bonferroni-corrected p-value <0.05.

text.text: Given the limited number of biological samples recruited in our cohort and the associated risk of false-positive results, two distinct sensitivity analyses were employed to assess the robustness of the primary findings: (i) a non-parametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test, which minimises reliance on the distributional assumptions required by negative binomial regression; and (ii) a generalised negative binomial linear mixed model (implemented using lme4 [v1.1.37] (35)) adjusting for the same covariates described above (fixed effects) and fitting individual as a random effect, to account for non-independence of subject-specific gene expression measures.
Significant and high-confidence cluster-specific DE genes were finally determined if they satisfied the Bonferroni-corrected significance thresholds in both sensitivity analyses.

High-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA [v0.4.9]) (36) was utilised to construct cluster-specific gene co-expression modules in each cluster in which every sample contributed at least 75 cells.
text.formatted: High-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA [v0.4.9]) <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(36)</ref> was utilised to construct cluster-specific gene co-expression modules in each cluster in which every sample contributed at least 75 cells.

text.text: Metacells were generated with k = 25 (number of nearest neighbour cells pooled to form each metacell) and max_shared = 10 (maximum number of constituent cells any two metacells may share, limiting overlap and redundancy).
Clusters were retained for network inference only if they contained at least 100 metacells per treatment group to improve the stability of gene-gene correlation estimates.

The soft thresholding power was selected as the smallest value at which the scale free topology model fit plateaued and median connectivity stabilised, which was used to transform the signed gene-gene correlations into a scale free adjacency matrix.
This adjacency matrix was then converted to the topological overlap matrix and subjected to hierarchical clustering to define co expression modules.

For each detected module, the module eigengene was computed as the first principal component of the module's gene expression matrix across metacells that served as the module's representative profile.

To identify cluster-specific gene co-expression modules associated with CIN status and treatment for TRS with CIN and TRS without CIN separately, differential module eigengene (DME) analyses were performed using generalised linear regression, applying the same comparisons and covariate adjustments as in the DE analysis described above.
Module eigengenes were normalised using an inverse rank based transformation.
Similarly, two sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess robustness: (i) a non-parametric Wilcoxon ranksum test and (ii) a generalised linear mixed model.
Cluster specific co expression modules were deemed significant and high confidence if they met the Bonferroni corrected significance threshold in both sensitivity analyses.
For each significant co-expression module identified, transcription factor (TF) regulatory network analysis was performed to elucidate the regulatory architecture underlying the corresponding module.
Candidate cis-regulatory elements were mapped by scanning the human genome (hg38) for motifs curated from the JASPAR 2024 CORE vertebrate collection (37).
text.formatted: Candidate cis-regulatory elements were mapped by scanning the human genome (hg38) for motifs curated from the JASPAR 2024 CORE vertebrate collection <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(37)</ref>.

text.text: Regulatory networks were inferred using gradient-boosted regression (via XGBoost), in which target gene expression was modelled as a function of TF activity.

TF-gene pairs were quantified using regulatory scores derived from the model's feature importance metrics, reflecting the relative contribution of each TF to predicting its target gene expression while accommodating combinatorial regulation by multiple TFs.
Functional regulons were defined at the TF level as sets of high confidence target genes, retaining TF-gene pairs with regulatory scores greater than 0.05.
For each regulon, aggregated activity scores were computed across cells using the RegulonScores algorithm, restricted to target genes showing absolute correlation >0.10 with the corresponding TF.
text.formatted: For each regulon, aggregated activity scores were computed across cells using the RegulonScores algorithm, restricted to target genes showing absolute correlation >0.10 with the corresponding TF.

text.text: The regulon activity scores were further stratified into positively and negatively co expressed sub-networks to distinguish transcriptional activation and repression.
Activity regulon scores were normalised using an inverse rank based transformation.

Associations between transformed activity regulon scores and CIN/treatment status were evaluated using the same analytical framework (i.e., combining generalised linear regression with sensitivity analyses) as was applied in the DME framework.
Module-specific regulons were considered significant if they met the Bonferronicorrected significance threshold consistently across all models.

Six participants (aged 22-60 years) with a diagnosis of schizophrenia and a history of previous clozapine treatment were recruited: three were classified into the CIN group (TRS with CIN: 1 female, 2 males), and three into the clozapine-exposed control group (TRS without CIN: 3 males).
Participants in the clozapine-exposed control group had ceased clozapine due to adverse effects (sedation, n = 2) and difficulty maintaining long-term adherence (n = 1).
Smoking status were also recorded: three participants were smokers (2 TRS with CIN, 1 TRS without CIN) and three were non-smokers (1 TRS with CIN, 2 TRS without CIN).

PBMCs were collected from each participant and treated under three conditions: untreated, clozapine, and clozapine + metabolites, yielding a total of 18 donortreatment combinations (hereafter "samples").
Two samples (i.e., one TRS with CIN and one TRS without CIN, both treated with clozapine) were randomly excluded from the downstream snRNA-seq data generation.
Following the application of stringent QC filters (Figures S1-4), a total of 59,313 single nuclei remained for analysis.

Finally, cell-cell communication analysis revealed seven ligand-receptor (L-R) pairs.

Five of these ("CD99-CD99", "CD99-PILRB", "CLEC2B-KLRB1", "CLEC2D-KLRB1", "ICAM2-(ITGAL+ITGB2)") showed significantly different communication probabilities between TRS with vs without CIN (Figure 5A and Table S12).

text.text: All five L-R pairs mediated communication among CD4 T cells, CD8 T cells, and NK cells.

Specifically, "CLEC2B-KLRB1" and "CLEC2D-KLRB1" signalling originated from naïve CD4/CD8 T cells and NK cells (NKG2D high) and converged on NK cells (terminal differentiation), whereas memory CD4 T cells (Th-differentiation) and NK cells (terminal differentiation) were the main sources of "CD99-CD99", "CD99-PILRB", and "ICAM2-(ITGAL+ITGB2)" signalling.

The two remaining L-R pairs ("CD55-ADGRE5" for clozapine alone and "SELPLG-SELL" for clozapine + metabolites) were significantly associated with clozapine response (vs. untreated) in TRS with CIN but not in TRS without CIN (Figure 5B and Table S12).

Conversely, no L-R pairs showed significant changes that were specific to TRS without CIN, and no significant L-R pairs were identified specific to clozapine + metabolites (vs. clozapine), consistent with our earlier analyses.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first human single nucleus RNA-seq study to characterise PBMC-based cellular transcriptomic changes associated with CIN and response to clozapine and its two major metabolites in TRS with and without CIN.

We identified a set of cell type-specific differentially expressed (DE) genes associated with CIN status, as well as DE genes that respond to clozapine (and its metabolites) in TRS with CIN, but not TRS without CIN, most of which have not been reported in prior GWAS of CIN.
Co-expression analyses provided convergent evidence for a central role of a naïve CD4 T cell (inflammatory response)-specific module in TRS with CIN, potentially regulated by the SREBF1.
Pathway analysis implicated cytokine and interferon-gamma responses, transcriptional repression, and cadherin and nucleotide binding underlying this co-expression module.

Additionally, CD99-, CLEC-, and ICAM-associated L-R pairs were implicated in association with TRS with CIN, while SELPLG-and ADGRE-associated L-R pairs were linked to clozapine response in TRS with CIN only, across multiple cell type interactions, suggesting altered intercellular communication in CIN and following clozapine exposure.

The key contribution of this study is the generation of the first single nucleus transcriptomic landscape of PBMCs for response to clozapine and its two major metabolites in TRS with and without CIN, resolving 26 distinct immune cell populations and a list of 57 cell typespecific DE genes associated with CIN status and exposure to clozapine and/or its metabolites.
Among the CIN-associated genes, FAM118A and IL32 were notable for being significantly differentially expressed across multiple immune cell types.

FAM118A encodes a noncanonical human sirtuin protein that depletes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) when overexpressed (41), which has the potential to impact NAD-dependent granulopoiesis (42).
text.formatted: FAM118A encodes a noncanonical human sirtuin protein that depletes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) when overexpressed <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(41)</ref>, which has the potential to impact NAD-dependent granulopoiesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(42)</ref>.

text.text: We found that FAM118A was consistently upregulated in naïve CD4 and CD8 T cells and NK cells in TRS with CIN, suggesting that increased FAM118A expression may disrupt NAD-dependent signals that support neutrophil production.

IL32 encodes a pro-inflammatory cytokine that induces TNF-α and IL-8 (43, 44), and binds proteinase 3, a serine protease abundantly expressed in neutrophils (45), suggesting a potential link between lymphocyte activation and neutrophil function.

Beyond these CIN-associated genes, we identified a distinct set of cell type-specific DE genes associated with exposure to clozapine and/or clozapine + metabolites in TRS donors with CIN but not in TRS without CIN.
Two of the identified genes, DDX5 and UBA52 are of particular interest.
DDX5 acts as a transcriptional corepressor that restricts the suppressive activity of RORγt regulatory T cells by reducing IL-10 production (46).

UBA52 was also associated with CIN status when comparing TRS with CIN to TRS without CIN, but in different cell types and with inconsistent direction of expression change, suggesting context-dependent regulation rather than serving as a fixed marker of neutropenia.

text.text: The direction of these correlations is consistent with our expectations: CIN-associated transcriptional alterations should align with clozapine-related changes in TRS with CIN, whereas the relationship is anticipated to be reversed in TRS without CIN.

The same pattern held for analyses involving response to clozapine + metabolites, whereas it was weaker for the direct comparison of clozapine alone with clozapine + metabolites (TRS with CIN: = 0.03, pvalue = 1.30×10 -11 ; TRS without CIN: = 0.06, p-value = 1.80×10 -34 ).
This suggests that a shared transcriptional signal exists but is too subtle for individual genes to pass stringent multiple-testing correction in either analysis.
Differences in study design and statistical power, together with cell type-specific effects, may further obscure this overlap.
Validation in larger cohorts will be needed to confirm and characterise this shared signal.
Furthermore, we identified a module in naïve CD4 T cells (inflammatory response) that was associated with CIN status and potentially regulated by the transcription factor SREBF1.
The top hub genes in this module form a prominent functional group comprising genes involved in translation initiation and elongation, including EEF1G, EEF2, and EEF1B2.
The eEF1B complex (EEF1B2, EEF1G) regenerates eEF1A-GTP to sustain aminoacyl-tRNA delivery during elongation (54), and EEF2 drives ribosomal translocation that is regulated by mTORC1 signalling (55).

text.text: Together, these findings suggest altered immune-cell adhesion and trafficking programmes in TRS with CIN.
Our findings have important clinical implications.
Despite its superior efficacy in TRS, clozapine remains underutilised, partly due to concerns regarding serious adverse effects such as CIN (69).

text.text: Current management of CIN typically involves clozapine withdrawal, with potential for cautious rechallenge if alternative contributing factors are identified and addressed.
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and lithium have shown promise in supporting neutrophil counts during clozapine rechallenge (70).
text.formatted: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and lithium have shown promise in supporting neutrophil counts during clozapine rechallenge <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(70)</ref>.

text.text: However, a major clinical challenge remains the inability to predict which individuals are susceptible to CIN or its recurrence.
Our findings support an immune-mediated mechanism underlying CIN and identify candidate cell type-specific genes and pathways that may play a role in susceptibility.

Furthermore, by characterising cell-specific responses, our study identifies candidate mechanisms that may inform the development of targeted therapeutic strategies to prevent CIN before clinically significant neutropenia develops.

Such advances could facilitate the safe continuation or reintroduction of clozapine in individuals with TRS, for whom effective treatment alternatives remain limited, with potentially life-saving implications.
Our findings should be interpreted in the context of several limitations.

First, we used the 10X Genomics Fixed RNA Profiling platform for snRNA-seq, which excludes hypervariable genes in the HLA region, a well-known genetic locus associated with clozapine response; this may have constrained our ability to detect all relevant associations.
Second, our study including only three TRS donors with CIN and three without, primarily due to the low prevalence of CIN and the recruitment challenges inherent to a severely ill patient cohort.

Consequently, the study lacks the statistical power to detect cell type-specific DE genes, coexpression modules, and pathways with small effect sizes, and we cannot entirely account for the influence of confounding variables such as age, sex and smoking.

Consistent with this limitation, intersecting the 57 significant cell type-specific DE genes identified in our study with MAGMA gene-based results from GWAS of CIN (17) yielded no overlap after multipletesting correction (Supplementary Methods, Table S14).

text.text: Larger cohorts will be necessary to validate and expand upon these preliminary findings.
Third, we only focused on the two major clozapine-related metabolites.
Potential effects of other bioactivated or downstream metabolites of clozapine remain to be defined and warrant systematic evaluation.
Finally, the lack of an independent replication cohort necessitates caution in the interpretation of the results.
In summary, this study provides the first single nucleus transcriptomic characterisation of immune cell type-specific responses to clozapine and its two major metabolites in TRS with and without CIN.

We identified a set of cell type-specific DE genes, predominantly in naïve CD4 and CD8 T cells, a naïve CD4 T cell-specific co-expression module, and five intercellular L-R pairs that was associated with TRS with CIN compared to TRS without CIN.
We also identified distinct cell type-specific DE genes and L-R pairs involved in response to clozapine in TRS with CIN but not TRS without CIN.
While several DE genes, such as FAM118A and DDX5, provide biologically plausible links to neutropenia-relevant mechanisms, these associations remain exploratory pending validation.

Future studies should replicate these findings in larger, independent cohorts, including prospective sampling before clozapine initiation and comparison against other immune-mediated drug-induced agranulocytosis, to establish both temporality and specificity.

Functional evaluation of the implicated pathways in naïve CD4 T cells co-cultured with metabolite-pulsed autologous antigen-presenting cells would test whether the observed transcriptional state modifies the activation threshold to clozapine-derived antigen.

Ultimately, with sufficient validation, these findings may contribute to the long-term development of a clinical tool for stratifying CIN risk in patients with TRS, potentially informing more tailored clinical monitoring.   expressed (DE) genes that passed Bonferroni correction and remained significant in both sensitivity analyses are highlighted.
